To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk for cardiovascular morbidity in people with type 2 Diabetes and drug-treated hypertension increases with blood pressure reduction below 120/80 and above 140/90 mm Hg.
the risk of macrovascular events in type 2 diabetic patients with hypertension is J-shaped and that the risk is higher in those with SBP ⩽120  and ⩾140 mmHg than in those with SBPs of 120–140 mmHg.
the risk for CVD events was increased in patients with T2D and hypertension with SBP ⩽120 and⩾140 Hg compared with those with 130⩼SBP<140 Hg.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the J-shaped phenomenon in patients with diabetes with hypertension.
the relationship between SBP and risk of CVC events in patients with T2D and drug-treated hypertension.
a J-shaped phenomenon in the risk of CVD in patients with diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a BP reduction below the range of 120–140 mm Hg is not recommended.
the relationship between BP and CVD risk is not linear and there is still a need to find a better strategy for CVD risk management in people with diabetes.
a SBP⫽120 mm Hg and a DBP⫽80 mm HG are associated with a higher risk for macrovascular complications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of CVD and CHDs is inversely related to BP reduction below the normal level of 120 mm g for those with T2D.
a SBP of 120–140 mm  Hg is associated with a lower CVD risk compared with a SBP of <120 or >140 mm hg in people with diabetes.
the risk for CVD events in people with diabetes and hypertension is not only associated with the BP level but also related to its reduction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of CVD and CHDs in patients with diabetes with hypertension is not linear.
the J-shaped phenomenon is a real entity, which is more pronounced in patients with T2D and drug-treated hypertension.
the risk of CVD in patients with diabetes is not linearly associated with BP reduction.
